question: Where can I find FAST-NUCES past papers for PF, Calculus, sessionals and finals?
answer:
Most FAST past papers you'll find online come from student-run archives rather than the university itself. A few of them are well organised, but quality and coverage vary, so it helps to know what you're opening before you start solving.

The one most people begin with is the Islamabad campus computing archive on GitHub. Search for nuces-isb-past-papers and it comes up. It's laid out as semester, then course, then department, with folders for all eight semesters and a separate folder of course outlines. Files are named by subject, sessional or final, and the term and year, so you can tell what you're opening before you click. If your course has no folder, it usually just means nobody has uploaded papers for it yet. You can ask for it by opening an issue, or add papers yourself through a pull request, which the maintainers check before merging.

If you're in first semester at Karachi, look for FAST-KHI-Semester-1 under the FAST-NUCES-Hub account. It has separate folders for PF theory and PF lab, Calculus, Applied Physics, Functional English, ICT and Islamic Studies, and the same author links to repositories for semesters two to five. It was put together around one study plan, so compare it with the courses you're actually registered in instead of assuming it matches.

There's also a student archive called Academic Time Machine that started at the Lahore campus and has been forked by other students, so you'll come across a few versions of it.

Before you trust any paper, check four things: the campus, the exact course, the year, and whether it's Sessional I, Sessional II or a final. Keep those separate. A final from a few years back covers topics you probably haven't reached before your first sessional, and a paper from another campus is good extra practice but doesn't tell you how your own instructor will set the exam. Open the file before relying on its name. Make sure the heading matches the folder and that all the pages are there. If a solution is attached, find out whether it's a marking scheme or just a student's attempt. Student answers can be wrong, so ask your TA about anything that looks off.

How you use papers matters more than how many you collect. Here's a simple way to do it. Take the last two or three papers of the same type from your campus and sort the questions by topic. Notice which topics keep coming back, then compare that list with what your instructor has actually covered. Now you have a priority list built from the pattern and your real syllabus. Attempt the questions before you look at any solutions, then compare, note the concepts you missed and go back to them. Reading a solution and nodding along feels like progress, but it's only recognition, and that isn't the same as being able to do it on a blank page.

One caution. Past papers means papers from exams that have already been held. Getting a question paper before an exam is a different thing altogether. FAST's rules treat paying for early access to a paper as extreme dishonesty, and the penalty is expulsion. It's never worth it.

If your course isn't covered anywhere, ask seniors who took it recently, ideally with the same instructor, and see what they kept. No archive has every semester, and none can tell you what your next paper will look like.

question: How should I prepare for FAST sessional exams, and are lecture slides enough?
answer:
Slides on their own usually aren't enough. No rule says so, since it depends on the course and the instructor, but slides only tell you what was covered. They can't tell you whether you can actually solve something with it, and that's exactly what a sessional tests.

Start with the dates. FAST announces the sessional and final exam weeks at the start of the semester, and you're not allowed to miss them. A missed exam gets no credit unless you qualify for a retake, and that needs a real emergency with documents. So work backwards from the date instead of waiting for the week before. Keep in mind too that in-semester work normally makes up half of a course's marks, with the final carrying the other half, so a bad sessional isn't something you can just write off. Check your own course outline for the exact split.

Next, build a topic checklist from your instructor's outline and what has actually been taught. Beside each topic, be honest with yourself. Can I explain this? Can I solve a question on it without looking? Most people overestimate. The gaps you find are your revision plan, and anything that hasn't been taught yet stays off the list even if an old paper includes it.

How you practise depends on the course. In PF, write programs and trace code on paper instead of only reading it. In Calculus, work through the exercise sets listed in your outline and write out every step, because marks often depend on showing the method. In Applied Physics, a lot of the paper tends to be numericals, so practise problems with changed values and learn why a formula applies, not just the formula. For a reading-heavy course, close the slides, explain a topic in your own words, then check what you missed. These patterns come from how students describe their own courses, so your instructor's format is what counts.

Once you've reviewed a topic, use past papers as a timed rehearsal. Sit one under real conditions. Same time limit, no notes, no phone or smartwatch, and keep the solutions out of sight until you've made a serious attempt.

After marking your attempt, sort the mistakes into four kinds: you didn't know the concept, you knew it but applied it wrong, you misread the question, or you ran out of time. Each one needs a different fix. Extra reading won't help if you keep misreading questions, and speed drills won't fix a concept you never understood. Do this sorting after every paper, not after the fifth one.

A couple of habits to avoid. One is spending lecture time making beautiful notes instead of listening and understanding, which some students later list as a first-semester mistake. The other is putting all your effort into the courses you enjoy while the ones that need real work get left until the last minute.

If time is short, go for the confirmed syllabus first, then your weakest topics, and pay attention to what your instructor keeps stressing in class, since that tends to show up in exams.

Here's a check you can run the night before. Take a question you haven't seen, solve it, and explain why each step works. If you can only recognise a worked solution when you see it, you're not ready yet.

question: I understand Programming Fundamentals lectures but cannot solve FAST exam questions. How can I improve?
answer:
This is probably the most common first-semester problem at FAST, and it's fixable. Understanding a lecture and producing a solution from a blank page are two different skills. Lectures train the first one. Exams test the second, and the only way to build it is to practise producing solutions yourself.

PF is built around problem-solving, not memorising code. Students who've been through it keep saying the same few things: stay consistent, do more questions, and don't let your early momentum fade. Having coded before helps less than people expect, because the quizzes and midterms humble a lot of students who arrive with experience. The topics also carry forward. Pointers and dynamic memory come back in OOP and recursion comes back in data structures, so weak PF basics follow you for a long time.

Here's a routine that works for most people. Before you write any code, read the question and write down the input, the required output and any constraints. Then explain the steps in plain words, as if you were telling a friend how to do it by hand. Only after that, turn the steps into code in the language your course uses. When you get stuck, name exactly where. Is it understanding the question, choosing an approach, turning the approach into code, or finding a bug? Each one has a different fix, and knowing which one it is saves hours.

Mix up your practice. Solve something from an empty page. Trace a short program line by line and write down what each variable holds at every step. Take a broken solution and explain why it fails before you fix it. If your exams are handwritten, practise on paper as well, then type it in afterwards, compile it and see what you got wrong. When you fix an error, make sure you can say why it was an error. Changing things until the output looks right teaches you nothing.

For extra questions, easy problems on sites like LeetCode or HackerRank are fine once the basics are in place. Past papers work best after you've got a grip on the concepts, as a test of what's still shaky rather than as your first resource.

You'll also find older PF assignment sets from Lahore (Fall 2022, theory course) on GitHub with student solutions. Use the questions selectively, check they match what your instructor has covered, and don't open the solutions until you've tried. They're old and student-written, they're not an answer key, and they're for theory, not labs.

A word on AI. Under FAST's rules, AI tools are generally off-limits in labs like PF, OOP and data structures unless your lab instructor explicitly allows them. Even where they are allowed, copying code you don't understand catches up with you at the first midterm. If you use an AI tool to explain a concept while studying, check what it told you, then close it and solve the problem again on your own.

Don't treat one bad result as the end of the story. A single lab exam or quiz is only part of the semester's marks, and plenty of students find the first lab exam rough. What helps is going to your instructor or TA with your attempted solution and one specific question. 'I don't see why this step works' gets a far better answer than 'I can't do PF'. The best measure of progress is what you can solve and explain without help, not how many videos you've watched.

question: Can I still get a 3.0 or higher GPA at FAST after bad mids?
answer:
It might be possible, but a midterm on its own doesn't tell you where you'll end up. Before you decide anything, find out four things for each course: how the marks are split, how much you've already earned, how much is still to come, and how your instructor turns the final total into a letter grade. At FAST, in-semester work (midterms, assignments, quizzes) normally makes up 50% of a course and the final exam makes up the other 50%, but check your own course outline because a few courses differ.

Here's the maths. Take every assessment that has been marked and convert it to its weighted share:

weighted marks = marks earned / marks available x weight of that assessment

Add those up and you know what's already in the bank. Then pick a target total for the course, say 70 out of 100. What you need on the rest is:

required average on remaining work = (target total - marks in the bank) / marks still available x 100

Here's an example. Say the course is out of 100, with 50 marks of semester work and a 50-mark final. So far 30 marks of the semester work have been marked and you've earned 12 of them. That leaves 20 marks of semester work plus the final, 70 marks in all. To finish on 70 overall you need 58 of those 70, about 83%. That's hard but not impossible. If the number had come out at 95%, you'd know to put your energy somewhere else.

One catch is that this gives you a course total, not a grade. Your instructor decides how totals become letter grades, so ask how it's done instead of guessing. If your course is graded relative to the class, being near the average on one midterm tells you even less. Don't plan around rumours about scaling.

Now the GPA side. Your semester GPA is weighted by credit hours, so a 3-credit course counts for more than a 1-credit lab. The grade points are A+ and A 4.00, A- 3.67, B+ 3.33, B 3.00, B- 2.67, C+ 2.33, C 2.00, C- 1.67, D+ 1.33, D 1.00 and F 0.00. A 3.00 semester doesn't need all B's. An A and a C in two courses of equal credit hours average out to exactly 3.00. In your first semester your CGPA is just your SGPA. After that it's the credit-weighted average of everything you've taken, and the early semesters give you the most room to move it. Lifting a 2.5 to a 3.0 in your second year is far easier than doing it in your last.

If you're thinking about repeating a course, remember the latest attempt replaces the earlier one in your CGPA, even if the new grade is lower. Summer repeats exist, but only for certain categories of students, so don't count on them as a safety net. And in your first semester you can't drop courses, so recovery has to come from doing better in what's left.

Now go through your marked paper properly. FAST's rules say evaluation material should be shared with students after marking, so ask to see it. For every lost mark, decide why. Missing concept, incomplete reasoning, misread question, or ran out of time. That list is your plan for the next assessment. Then keep track of everything still to come: quizzes, assignments, labs, the second sessional and the final. Assignment and lab marks are easy to neglect and they add up.

Check your marks online too. The Student Handbook makes it your responsibility to check recorded grades and report any discrepancy to the Academic Office, and it says grades won't be changed if you don't report a problem in good time. If something looks wrong, say so quickly.

Last thing. Don't build your recovery on promises from friends that the next paper will be easy or that marks will be scaled up. Build it on the marks still available and what you do with them.

question: What happens if attendance falls below 80% at FAST, and how many classes can I miss?
answer:
Short version: at FAST, attendance isn't an 80% free pass. The rule is 100% attendance, and the Head of Department can condone up to 20% absence for genuine reasons such as illness. That's a decision someone makes after looking at your case, not an allowance you can spend on skipping classes. If you fall short in a course, you can't sit its final exam and you're given an FA grade. That counts as a fail with 0.00 grade points, and a failed course normally has to be repeated in the next semester it's offered.

You'll hear '80%' a lot. The number comes from that 20% limit on what can be condoned, and the rulebook also names an 80% attendance rule specifically for summer courses. For a regular semester, treat full attendance as the expectation.

So how many classes can you miss? There isn't one fixed number. The percentage is worked out from the sessions your department actually counts for that course, so it changes with how many sessions there are. If every session counts equally, the arithmetic is:

attendance (%) = attended sessions / counted sessions x 100

and the most you could miss while staying at 80% is counted sessions x 0.20, rounded down. For example, with 32 counted sessions, 20% is 6.4, so 6 absences is the ceiling. A lab with 16 counted sessions gives 3. Treat that as arithmetic only, because your department's record decides, and how cancelled classes and make-up classes get counted can change the totals.

Labs deserve their own check. Their attendance is recorded separately, so strong attendance in your other courses doesn't cover a shortage in a lab. Labs also have fewer sessions, so each absence takes a bigger bite out of the percentage, and students often get caught out by that.

If you're already below 80%, first separate where you are now from where you could still end up. Take the department's confirmed counts and add all the remaining sessions to both your attended number and the total. That shows the highest percentage still possible. If even perfect attendance from here would leave you short, go to the Academic Office or your HoD straight away, not at the end of the semester.

The process matters as much as the numbers. The Student Handbook says that if you miss classes for an unavoidable reason, you should inform the Academic Office within two days and list any assignments or quizzes you missed. Late applications aren't entertained. It also makes you responsible for checking your own attendance every week and reporting any discrepancy immediately. So look at your attendance weekly, not once at the end. Keep any evidence, such as medical papers, and follow the official process.

If the record is simply wrong, get it corrected through the Academic Office. A classmate's assurance or an online calculator can't authorise an exception, so don't rely on either.
